verses.1: A psalm by David, which he sang to the LORD regarding the words of Cush, the son of Bennai.
verses.2: LORD, my God, in you I have taken refuge. Rescue me from all my pursuers and deliver me.
verses.3: Lest like a lion he tear my soul, devouring it with no one to save.
verses.4: LORD, my God, if I have done this— if there is iniquity in my hands—
verses.5: if I have repaid evil to the one who was at peace with me, or if I have robbed the one who had no quarrel with me—
verses.6: let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it, let him crush my life to the ground and lay my glory in the dust. Selah.
verses.7: Arise, LORD, in your anger; rise up against the rage of my foes and stir me to judgment that you have commanded.
verses.8: And the assembly of peoples shall surround you; from on high, return to it.
verses.9: The LORD will judge peoples. Judge me, LORD, according to my righteousness and according to the integrity that is in me.
verses.10: Let evil come to an end for the wicked, and let the righteous be established, for you are the one who examines hearts and minds, O God.
verses.11: My shield is with God, the one who saves the upright in heart.
verses.12: God is the judge of the righteous and the God who is wrathful every day.
verses.13: If he does not turn back, his sword is sharpened, his bow is drawn and made ready.
verses.14: And he has prepared weapons of death; his arrows are for blazing ones, ready to fly.
verses.15: Behold, he conceives iniquity, bears trouble, and gives birth to falsehood.
verses.16: He has dug a pit and dug it out, and he himself will fall into the trap he has made.
verses.17: His labor will return on his head, and his violence will descend upon his own brow.
verses.18: I will give thanks to the LORD for his righteousness and sing praise to the name of the LORD Most High.

notes:
Notes
- v. 6: “Selah” is retained as a musical or liturgical marker, commonly understood but not fully explained in the Hebrew text.
- v. 10: “examine hearts and minds” reflects the dual terms for internal organs in Hebrew, which are often used metaphorically for moral character.
